items.title: Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to cast ballot in US election
items.image_alt: Pope Leo leads the Angelus prayer from the window of the Apostolic Palace at the Vatican, October 11, 2026. Vatican Media/Elisabetta Trevisan/Handout via REUTERS
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Pope Leo XIV cast a ballot by mail in the US midterm elections, the Vatican press office said on Friday, a historic first for the American-born pontiff.

"In keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago," the Vatican said. "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes."

The Vatican did not say which candidates Leo had voted for.

Leo, 71, was born in Chicago and is the first American-born pope. The pope voted by mail under his birth name, Robert Francis Prevost, according to the Will County Clerk's website.

President Donald Trump's sagging popularity is hurting his fellow Republicans' chances of holding onto their majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 election, with the public unhappy about the high cost of living and the Iran war.

Trump repeatedly criticized Leo early in the new pope's tenure, calling him "weak" and "terrible" on crime.

The pope said in March that God rejects the prayers of those who start wars and have "hands full of blood." In April, he termed Trump's threat to destroy the Iranian civilization as unacceptable and previously declined to join the US president's so-called "Board of Peace" initiative for Gaza.

Leo has also urged a "deep reflection" on the way migrants are treated in the US.

Voters in the solidly Democratic state of Illinois will select a successor for retiring US Senator Dick Durbin and choose whether to re-elect Governor JB Pritzker.

Leo was elected to lead the 1.4-billion-member Church by the world's cardinals in May 2025.

The pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on October 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Doctors say he will not need further therapy.

He is set to travel to South America next week.

items.title: FBI and US Secret Service working with Binance after $6.3 billion hack, source says

image.alt: Representations of cryptocurrencies are seen in front of displayed Binance logo in this illustration taken November 10, 2022. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo

items.content_html:
LONDON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - Binance is working with law enforcement around the world, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the United States Secret Service (USSS), after hackers stole a record $6.3 billion from the platform, a person familiar with the situation told Reuters.

The FBI said in a statement that it was "aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps."

The USSS did not respond to a request for comment sent via email outside of US hours.

Reporting by Elizabeth Howcroft and AJ Vicens in Detroit; Editing by Tommy Reggiori Wilkes and Chizu Nomiyama

items.title: On again: Trump restores weekend campaign rallies in Iowa, Kansas
items.image_alt: US President Donald Trump arrives at a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, US, October 22, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump has restored canceled campaign rallies in Iowa and Kansas days before November 3 midterm elections, a White House official said on Friday.

"Rallies are BACK ON! President Trump loves his supporters, and in addition to nearly 20 tele-rallies, he will hold back-to-back rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday," the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The reversal comes after Trump told reporters on Thursday he did not "feel like I have to go to Kansas," where Republican Senator Roger Marshall faces an unexpectedly competitive race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. "He is doing very well. We are going to have a strong Tuesday night," Trump said at the time.

The White House official said the rallies had been rearranged to accommodate the tele-rallies recently added to Trump's schedule.

On Friday, Trump will campaign in Florida, hoping to galvanize his supporters in a state he won handily in 2024 but where early voting has tilted toward Democrats.

It will be his latest stop in a state Republicans usually expect to win, following campaign events earlier this week in Mississippi and South Carolina.

Reporting by Jarrett Renshaw, Writing by Doina Chiacu; Editing by Michelle Nichols

items.title: Trump cancels weekend rallies, plans to phone in to other midterm campaign events
items.image_alt: US President Donald Trump delivers remarks at a midterm election campaign rally for incumbent US Senator Darline Graham (R-SC) at an event center in Rock Hill, South Carolina, US, October 29, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst
items.content_html:
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Maryland, Oct 29 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Thursday canceled planned weekend campaign stops in Kansas and Iowa, and his allies said he would instead phone in to rallies nationwide after four weeks of travel to boost Republicans' election chances.

Trump told reporters he did not "feel like I have to go to Kansas," a Midwestern state where Senator Roger Marshall, a fellow Republican, is in an unexpectedly competitive race with Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. "He is doing very well," Trump said of Marshall. "We are going to have a strong Tuesday night."

Later on Thursday, the Republican National Committee said in a statement that it would also cancel a planned rally in Iowa, home to several competitive congressional races.

The canceled in-person rallies were set for Salina, Kansas, on Saturday, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday.

Since October 1, Trump has hosted 25 rallies in 19 states, often speaking for his party in rural areas of Republican-friendly states. Tuesday's midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain narrow control of the US Senate and House of Representatives.

MAGA Inc, a campaign funding group aligned with Trump, said on Thursday it would host a series of "tele-rallies" with the president in at least 19 states, including Kansas and Iowa, before Election Day.

The president is still expected to travel to rallies in several states before Tuesday's election, including in Florida on Friday.

Trump has noted that his recent series of more than hour-long campaign speeches has been challenging. Sounding hoarse in Mississippi on Monday, Trump said, "God didn't make your vocal cords to do a rally every day."

On Thursday, after campaigning for Senator Darline Graham in South Carolina, Trump ridiculed a Reuters reporter who asked how he felt after weeks of rallies and whether he was sick of traveling.

"You've been following me for two weeks," Trump said before boarding his motorcade back to the White House. "I feel perfect."

Reporting by Jacob Bogage, Bo Erickson and Trevor Hunnicutt; Editing by Colleen Jenkins and Rosalba O'Brien

items.title: Trump administration bolsters bid to block Alaska Senate certification

image.alt: Alaska Senate candidates debate. REUTERS/Kerry Tasker/File Photo

items.content_html:
• DOJ issues 40-plus subpoenas and document requests in Alaska election probe
  • Revised lawsuit cites second Sullivan in Senate race
  • Alaska dispute could leave Senate control unclear for weeks
  • Alaska governor orders probe of alleged Democratic spoilers

ROCK HILL, South Carolina, Oct 29 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration filed a revised lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block Alaska's election results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses and, according to a person familiar with the matter, issued more than 40 subpoenas and document requests in its probe.

The revised complaint by the US Justice Department cited a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Sullivan who could siphon votes from the incumbent. The Justice Department said the effort was intended to mislead voters and help elect Democratic candidate Mary Peltola.

The suit raises the prospect of a messy fight over a contest that could determine US Senate control in next Tuesday's midterm elections. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, while Democrats need a net gain of four seats.

“They orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” lawyers for the Justice Department wrote in their amended complaint, referring to a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who is on the ballot without a party affiliation.

Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy also called for a state investigation into the allegation and said in an interview with News Nation that any finding of illegality “may in fact impact whether someone is seated in the US Senate.”

Peltola's campaign did not immediately respond to the amended complaint but has previously said it had “no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”

The Times reported on Wednesday that Peltola aides worked with campaign lawyers and staff at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to recruit two candidates who could siphon votes from the incumbent Republican Sullivan, including Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August, told the Times that Peltola was aware of the effort.

The DSCC has denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up candidates of their own in other races. Reuters was unable to independently verify the Times report.

Daniel J. Sullivan has previously denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.

TRUMP HAD PUSHED THE CASE

Trump, who for years has sowed doubts about the fairness of US elections, had pushed the Justice Department to bring the Alaska case even before the Times report, seeking to preemptively block Alaska from certifying Peltola, a former congresswoman, if she were to win the election.

Trump told reporters earlier on Thursday: “It's hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run. It's so unfair.”

Jessica Levinson, a professor who specializes in election law at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said that as long as Daniel J. Sullivan, the challenger to the incumbent, didn't conceal financial support, his campaign likely didn’t break any laws and political parties are allowed to mislead the public.

Policing such behavior would open the door to the government investigating why candidates choose to run and why voters support them, she said. “To the extent that people are uncomfortable with two Sullivans, I would offer you're probably going to be uncomfortable with a really high level of government intrusion into our elections as well.”

The Department of Justice has also escalated another legal campaign in California, where it has been investigating alleged voting by noncitizens.

The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's office received grand jury subpoenas as part of the probe, according to copies of subpoenas seen by Reuters on Thursday.

The subpoenas, dated last week, seek records related to the county's response to prior letters from the Trump administration warning of evidence that noncitizens are on the state's voter roll. They also seek documents about the county's efforts to prevent noncitizens from voting.

California has previously said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust.

A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment.

ELECTION DAY NEARS

As campaigning enters its final few days, the White House has shelved plans for Trump to appear on Saturday in Kansas, the site of an unexpectedly competitive Senate campaign, a Republican campaign official said.

“I don't feel like I have to go to Kansas,” Trump told reporters.

Instead, the president will participate in more than 20 virtual campaign appearances before Tuesday, a White House official said.

Trump held a rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Thursday, his second visit in two weeks to a state where opinion polls show an unexpectedly close Senate race between Republican Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews.

Speaking about the hotly contested Michigan Senate race, where progressive Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed holds a small lead in most polls over Republican Mike Rogers, Trump continued his identity-based attacks on El-Sayed, a Muslim, by saying at the rally that “if you're Black or if you're Jewish, and if you vote for Abdul, you're crazy.”

With control of the Senate at stake, both parties are deploying their biggest names in the closing days of the campaign, with Trump stumping for Republicans and former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning for Democrats in competitive races.

Harris stumped in Macon, Georgia, at a get-out-the-vote effort. Democrats are aiming to reelect Senator Jon Ossoff, who leads in polling, and hope that Keisha Lance Bottoms, locked in a tight race, can become the first woman elected as governor in the state.

Trump’s approval rating stood at 32% in a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday, near a record low, as Americans sour on the high cost of living and the war with Iran.

More than 44 million Americans had already voted as of Thursday evening, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million voted early in the 2022 midterms.

items.title: Judge says Trump bid to set aside California ballots would 'wreak havoc' on democracy
items.image_alt: An election sign encouraging people to vote is displayed in the front yard of a residential home in Encinitas, California, US, October 21, 2026. REUTERS/Mike Blake/File Photo
items.content_html:
Oct 28 (Reuters) - A US judge strongly rebuked the Trump administration on Wednesday by rejecting a request by the Justice Department to temporarily block California from counting mail ballots for the midterm elections from more than 20,000 registered voters the department alleges are likely noncitizens.

The decision marks the latest setback for President Donald Trump's effort to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress.

US District Judge David Carter issued the decision after a hearing on Tuesday in Los Angeles federal court over the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order barring officials from counting any ballots from the individuals it flagged.

The Justice Department's lawsuit, filed on October 15, was a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before an election and signaled the Trump administration's willingness to contest the midterm results in court.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," Carter wrote on Wednesday.

The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the Justice Department's last-minute request to exclude over 20,000 ballots ran afoul of "longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections."

Carter warned that a ruling in the Trump administration's favor would "wreak havoc" and cause thousands of registered voters to "potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve."

"Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable," Carter wrote. "Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger."

The Justice Department swiftly appealed the decision to the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals.

"Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials," Justice Department lawyer Bill Essayli said in a statement. "This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution."

California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data" and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state.

Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

Trump has repeatedly insisted that states are not doing enough to stop voting by noncitizens, which he says is widespread despite multiple studies and state audits showing it is rare.

APPEALS COURT REJECTED EMERGENCY REQUEST

Carter ruled two days after a federal appeals court on Monday rejected an unusual emergency request by the Justice Department asking the appeals court to temporarily block California from counting the ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.

The Justice Department did not indicate how many of the more than 20,000 people it flagged in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.

It had argued that a restraining order was necessary to ensure that California did not impede prosecutors' ability to enforce a federal law that makes it illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections.

But Carter said the Justice Department never explained why counting ballots would impair any prosecutions under the law, as states are not required to help the federal government investigate and prosecute crimes.

Apart from California, the Trump administration has sought to intervene in elections in two states that are home to competitive races.

In Alaska, the Justice Department last week asked a judge to prevent certification of election results if the Republican incumbent senator loses by a slim margin, alleging that the presence of another candidate with a similar name on the ballot could confuse voters. Alaska has urged that the case be dismissed, arguing it has taken steps to distinguish the two candidates on the ballot.

In Washington state, the Justice Department on Monday sent a letter asking officials not to count any ballots received from 400 voters it said may not be citizens. Washington's top elections official said the timing of the request indicated it was intended to cast unfounded suspicion on election results.

California had 23 million registered voters as of December 2025, while Washington had 5 million registered voters as of 2024, state records show.

Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the federal government's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizen voters risk wrongly flagging naturalized citizens for removal from the rolls.

items.title: US couple's retirement dream in ruins after residential cruise scrapped in Cambodia
items.image_alt: American couple Paul Montaya, 68, and Lynn Montaya, 64, from Colorado, U.S., who hoped to travel the world together while living aboard the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship, react during an interview with Reuters at their hotel after being forced to disembark in Cambodia, as the operator said rising fuel prices linked to conflict involving Iran had made operations prohibitively expensive, in Preah Sihanouk province, Cambodia, October 29, 2026. REUTERS/Soveit Yarn
items.content_html:
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Americans Lynn and Paul Montoya sold their house and cars in Wyoming so they could afford to buy a $179,000 cabin on the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey, plus roughly $6,000 a month in fees, to spend their retirement sailing the globe.

Their dream lasted 17 months on the ship before its operator abruptly announced this week that soaring fuel prices were forcing it to suspend operations. The company, Villa Vie Residences, informed the Montoyas and some 200 other passengers they had to disembark from the Odyssey at a port in Cambodia, along with pets and any personal items they could carry from their homes at sea.

"We really hadn't travelled that much out of the United States until probably a few months before we boarded the ship... and we just saw it as a great opportunity to be able to see the world," Paul told Reuters.

Uncertainty over the ship's future is more than just a travel hiccup for those who spent tens of thousands of dollars hoping to make it their home for years to come.

"They've run out of money," Paul said. "That's why they couldn't buy fuel. They've even had difficulties paying the crew on the ship, which even makes it more difficult. So we're really not expecting any money back."

Villa Vie did not respond to emailed questions or phone calls. In a statement on Tuesday, it said it was seeking to restructure and recapitalize, but no deals had been finalised.

"That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured," the company said, and added it was working to support those affected.

SIGNS MONEY WAS RUNNING OUT

As the war with Iran dragged on and fuel prices rose, Paul said residents noticed growing problems aboard the Odyssey. The company asked passengers to contribute more, and asked residents to provide a loan for fuel, he said.

"And then when we got to Cambodia, absolutely no internet," he said. "And the food quality began to deteriorate about three months ago, and we knew that the company was running out of money at that time."

The Montoyas said they now planned to live off the money they had budgeted for the monthly fees and spend some time in Malaysia.

Lynn said they would miss the community aboard the ship more than the lost money.

"It's hard to lose that money, but I also look at it as, we've had 17 months of going to the most amazing places and meeting the most amazing people," she said.

Reporting by Chantha Lach; Writing by Josh Smith; Editing by Alex Richardson

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US, Canada working on deal to ease steel, auto tariffs, sources say

image.alt: U.S. President Donald Trump meets with Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., October 7, 2025. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo

items.content_html:
OTTAWA/WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The United States and Canada are working on a deal to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, two US and four Canadian sources said, as the two governments try to repair relations that soured after trade talks broke down in August.

The talks focus on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including up to 50% tariff on Canadian steel and a 25% tariff on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties.

Just 32% of Americans approve of US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in next week's midterm elections. Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a political liability for Trump, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada.

One Canadian source briefed on the negotiations said a deal on steel and auto tariffs was possible before the November 3 elections, while US sources said the Trump administration wanted Canada to make further concessions. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because the talks are private.

The Section 232 tariffs are administered by the Commerce Department, putting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick rather than the US Trade Representative's office at the center of the negotiations, sources on both sides of the border said.

Lutnick and Canada's Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-US trade, have been in regular contact recently, one of the sources said.

"Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities," a spokesperson for LeBlanc said in a statement. "We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."

The US Trade Representative's Office and Canada have also been in contact in recent days regarding the overall architecture of any deal and all other trade issues, a USTR official said.

The White House and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

OTTAWA SEES PROGRESS

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said there had been "a slight intensification" in talks with the United States, adding that Ottawa had not changed its stance.

"To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position," he told reporters, but did not give details.

A Canadian industry source said a deal could come quickly, but not necessarily a broad one. "If it happens, it'll happen fast. But my sense is it'll be a narrowed deal, if it even happens," the source said.

Another Canadian source said they have believed for some time that a deal on Section 232 tariffs is likely before the midterms. Any agreement would be driven by Trump and Carney, the source said, adding that both leaders had said a mutually beneficial deal is possible.

Carney has said he wants a good deal for Canada.

US and Canadian trade talks collapsed in August over issues such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories. US automakers had hoped the trade talks would deliver relief from Washington's original 25% tariffs that have raised the cost of shipping vehicles and parts across the border.

Trump has previously announced that he would raise the tariffs on steel and auto imports from Canada to 50% from January 1, 2027. At a political rally on Sunday, Trump predicted the trade dispute would be resolved "soon," without providing specifics.

Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit businesses in Maine.

Reporting by Promit Mukherjee and David Shepardson; Additional reporting by David Ljunggren and David Lawder; Editing by Caroline Stauffer and Sanjeev Miglani

items.title: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
items.image_alt: A person shops for groceries in New York City, U.S., August 26, 2026. REUTERS/Jeenah Moon/File Photo
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The US economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, shrugging off higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East as consumers maintained robust spending and businesses doubled down on investment in AI.

The better-than-expected increase in gross domestic product last quarter reported by the Commerce Department on Thursday was in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and deterioration in consumer sentiment.

The advance GDP report was published less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Economists said the strong growth, together with other data on Thursday showing inflation accelerating and broadening out in September, bolstered the argument for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December.

The US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."

"The consequences of an economy at full employment in addition to a historic capital expenditures expansion are on vivid display," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "If the Fed is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending ... stratospheric private non-residential investment and sizzling inflation data."

Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the quickest since the third quarter of 2025, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its first estimate of third-quarter GDP. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Fed officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower. The dollar slipped against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% rate in the July-September period, matching the second quarter's pace. It was largely driven by services, including healthcare, visits to restaurants and bars as well as hotel and motel stays.

There was a pullback in spending on goods like motor vehicles and household furniture. Higher-income households, whose wealth has been boosted by AI-related strength in the stock market, are driving much of the spending.

Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are also helping other households to sustain spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation. Households are also saving less and dipping into their nest eggs. The saving rate fell to 4.1% from 4.4% in the second quarter. It fell to 3.8% in September.

"Growth isn't enough to give American families economic security," said Kyle Moore, chief economist at the Century Foundation. "Most of that growth has been lopsided, focused on the AI buildout. Wages for the typical worker still aren't keeping up with increasing prices."

Business spending on equipment surged at a 20.9% rate, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020. That added 1.16 percentage points to GDP growth, the most in six years. Information processing equipment, mainly computers and peripheral equipment, made up the bulk of the contribution.

Business spending on intellectual property products grew at an 8.4% rate, adding just under half a percentage point to GDP growth, mostly coming from software and research and development. Robust consumer and business spending were both sated with imports, which are a drag in the calculation of GDP.

Imports increased at a 19.7% rate, the quickest since the first quarter of 2025, when businesses were front-loading orders to avoid higher costs from Trump's sweeping tariffs.

LARGE DRAG FROM IMPORTS

Imports last quarter sliced off 2.64 percentage points from GDP growth, which was more than offset by the strength in consumer and business spending as well as a 1.61 percentage point contribution from the rebuilding of inventories, which had been drawn down for five straight quarters.

Government spending increased at a 5.3% rate amid a sharp rebound in federal government outlays, both defense and nondefense. Rising mortgage rates because of the Middle East conflict pushed residential investment back into contraction last quarter. Higher borrowing costs have overshadowed a moderation in house prices, weighing on demand for housing.

A measure of domestic demand, which excludes inventories, trade and government, accelerated at a 4.9% rate, the strongest since the second quarter of 2021. Final sales to private domestic purchasers grew at a 4.6% rate in the second quarter. Economists viewed the current pace of demand as unsustainable.

While inflation subsided last quarter as the cost of energy eased, price pressures picked up at the end of the third quarter.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index increased 0.5% in September after rising 0.3% in August, the BEA said in a separate report. In the 12 months through September, PCE inflation advanced 3.6% after rising 3.4% in August. It is one of the measures tracked by the Fed for its 2% inflation target. Rising inflation, with average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, left economists anticipating a slowdown in economic growth by year end.

Income at the disposal of households after accounting for inflation and taxes dropped 0.3% last month after being flat in August. Inflation-adjusted consumer spending was unchanged in September after rising 0.5% in August, putting consumption on a weaker growth path heading into the fourth quarter.

Economists also expected some moderation on AI-related spending as investors are focusing on the rising costs of long-term projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending.

"An economy increasingly supported by stock-market wealth and large technology projects also faces risks if share prices retreat or investment plans disappoint," said Sung Won Sohn, a finance and economics professor at Loyola Marymount University.

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama and Andrea Ricci

items.title: US Homeland Security cites risk to over 40,000 personnel in effort to take leaked data offline
items.image_alt: U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks near U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials during a press conference, to announce the success of Operation Rotten Apple, in New York City, U.S., September 1, 2026. REUTERS/David 'Dee' Delgado/File Photo
items.content_html:
Oct 29 (Reuters) - The US Department of Homeland Security asked an Icelandic hosting company on Thursday to take down or limit access to data related to thousands of agency personnel, saying the content put them at risk, according to the request posted online by hosting company FlokiNET.

The database “places more than 40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking, and physical harm,” the request said.

ZeroFox, a company authorized by the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency to pursue content removal actions, cited the figure in an email to FlokiNET.

FlokiNET CEO Kolja Weber told Reuters that his company would not remove the DHS data because it included government employee work addresses and work phone numbers, not personal phone numbers and addresses.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.”

Nonprofit data transparency group DDoSecrets released data on more than 40,000 DHS personnel on its website on Wednesday, alongside a separate, searchable database developed by hacker and journalist “maia arson crimew.” The database was briefly inaccessible on Thursday but was soon republished at a different domain.

A group calling itself “Department of Peace” claimed responsibility for obtaining the data, and said in a statement on Wednesday that DHS employees “have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped the data “can be used to limit further harm by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction.”

Privacy advocates have criticized DHS' use of personal data from other agencies, including Medicaid records and taxpayer data, for immigration enforcement.

Reporting by AJ Vicens in Detroit; Editing by Nia Williams and Rod Nickel

items.title: Warsh says politics played no role in Fed's rate decision by group he is 'honored' to lead
items.image_alt: US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh holds a press conference, following a two-day meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), at the Federal Reserve in Washington, DC, US, October 28, 2026. REUTERS/Kylie Cooper
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Wednesday said he is "honored" to lead the central bank's policymakers and said politics played no role in their decision to skip a rate hike, rebutting at least indirectly President Donald Trump's allegation that the Fed Board is partisan and against him.

"We just came out of a heck of a family fight" at the latest Federal Open Market Committee meeting, Warsh told reporters after the Fed ended a two-day meeting with a decision to leave the policy rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range.

"I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment, and I'm honored to be here and honored to be the chairman of this group," he said.

"Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh added. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics. I didn't hear a reference to politics, elections, what's happening in the next week."

Elections to be held on November 3 will determine if Trump's Republican Party retains its majorities in the House and Senate. Voters say affordability concerns, exemplified both by ongoing inflation as well as high borrowing costs, are top of mind as they head to the polls.

Warsh said he and his colleagues will get plenty of data in coming weeks that will leave them "better positioned" in December to determine whether to raise rates, and though the coming period will be "information-rich," it will have "nothing to do" with politics.

Trump, during both his first and second terms in the White House, has excoriated the central bank for failing to deliver big rate cuts, and after the Fed's decision in September to raise rates blamed Warsh's colleagues as "hostile" and "partisan."

Trump has not attacked Warsh himself, as he routinely did the previous Fed Chair Jerome Powell, and on Wednesday Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both he and the president have "great confidence that Chair Warsh will steer the Fed between the right combination of growth and inflation."

On Wednesday, Trump told reporters he had not spoken with Warsh about the central bank's decision.

Still, Wednesday's news conference demonstrated the minefield Warsh is traversing to remain in Trump's good graces while also trying to assure financial markets that he will credibly fight still-elevated inflation.

The administration continues to press the case against rate hikes, and Bessent told CNBC on Wednesday that while "some" on the Fed Board feel letting inflation stay so high for so long shows "a lack of will, I don't think it has to."

Fed Governor Lisa Cook was one of two dissenters on Wednesday's decision, preferring another quarter-point interest-rate hike instead of the hold that the Fed's 10 other rate-setters agreed to.

Trump has been trying to fire Cook for more than a year, with a possible White House administrative proceeding set for November 5, and has also called for Powell to vacate his seat on the central bank's Board of Governors. The two matters have high stakes for the Fed's status as an independent policy-making body.

Asked if he would be involved in the White House proceedings against Cook, however, Warsh said, "not to my knowledge."

Warsh was chosen by Trump to succeed Powell, who was also appointed by Trump to lead the Fed. Powell quickly fell afoul of the president for not following his advice on monetary policy.

As Warsh took over the Fed in late May, Trump said he was confident Warsh would lower rates and that he would not have selected him for the job if he did not feel that was the case.

Instead, persistent inflation and market doubts about Warsh's independence led the new Fed chief to take a hardline position in pledging to defend the Fed's 2% inflation target, with a rate hike in September and more considered likely.

So far, Trump has given Warsh the benefit of the doubt, blaming the rate rise on a group of governors appointed by former President Joe Biden that includes Cook.

items.title: US weekly jobless claims hover near 57-year lows
items.image_alt: Signage for a job fair is seen on 5th Avenue in Manhattan, New York City, U.S., September 3, 2021. REUTERS/Andrew Kelly
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits hovered near 57-year lows last week amid labor market resilience.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 1,000 to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended October 24, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 199,000 claims for the latest week.

Claims have stayed mostly below 200,000 since mid-September and are within striking distance of the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, which was the lowest reading since 1969.

Economists view the labor market as remaining in a "low-hire, low-fire" state. They said strong profits as domestic demand remains resilient were keeping layoffs near historic lows. But the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran was making employers hesitant to increase headcount, economists said.

The claims report showed the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, dropped 21,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.701 million during the week ended October 17.

The so-called continuing claims covered the week during which the government surveyed households for October's unemployment rate. The jobless rate was at 4.2% in September, and could remain steady or even edge down this month as a Conference Board survey on Tuesday showed consumers more optimistic about the labor market in October.

A reduction in the labor force amid the Trump administration's immigration crackdown is a key factor in keeping the unemployment rate low. The Federal Reserve on Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."

Economists expect the US central bank to raise rates in December. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh acknowledged the labor market stability, telling reporters that "on the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive."

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US DOJ is inquiring about Nvidia's purchase of Hugging Face, sources say
items.image_alt: NVIDIA logo is displayed on a screen at the NVIDIA GTC conference, in Berlin, Germany, October 21, 2026. REUTERS/Annegret Hilse
items.content_html:
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The US Department of Justice has made inquiries about how Nvidia's $12.93 billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face would affect competition in artificial intelligence, at the same time as antitrust enforcers pursue their years-long investigation into the chip designer's conduct, two people familiar with the matter said.

The Justice Department's recent questioning covers Nvidia's acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether the chip designer has exerted pressure on its customers, the two people said. On Hugging Face, Justice Department officials have asked whether the deal would let Nvidia capture a fundamental distribution point for AI, the people said. The acquisition is expected to close in the first half of 2027, Nvidia has said, adding that Hugging Face would continue to support work with a range of chip, cloud and AI providers.

The department's questions around the Hugging Face deal and details of its continued pursuit of Nvidia's conduct more broadly are reported for the first time here. Nvidia has become a cornerstone of the tech economy and AI boom, backing major players such as Anthropic and OpenAI while spurring data center development globally so its chips can power AI's voracious computing needs.

Any action by the DOJ could ripple through the chip industry and challenge Nvidia's investing and acquisition strategy that has extended its influence in AI. Government investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and do not necessarily result in lawsuits.

A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on any matters before the department, citing longstanding policy. The spokesperson added, "This DOJ under President Trump's leadership will continue to prioritize advancement of Super Intelligence for the betterment of the American people."

Nvidia declined to comment, and Hugging Face representatives did not respond to a request for comment.

The broad Nvidia examination started under former Democratic President Joe Biden and has continued under the administration of Republican President Donald Trump, during which time Nvidia has been the most valuable company in the world and a singular force in AI. There is no indication that Trump has any involvement, and the probe may not result in any Justice Department action.

As part of the probe, the DOJ has examined Nvidia's acquisition of SchedMD, one of the people said. The December 2025 purchase sparked worries among AI specialists about their access to SchedMD's open-source software, which helps run supercomputers relevant to national security. Nvidia has vowed to continue open access and support.

NVIDIA AND TRUMP

Nvidia has the biggest share of the market for AI chips, which power the likes of ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and similar tools. A host of startups and chip-design companies have challenged its dominance.

Competitors Broadcom and Alphabet's Google design processors together, seeking to beat Nvidia hardware with chips purpose-built for specific tasks and AI software. Advanced Micro Devices has said it can produce technically superior hardware and has struck billion-dollar deals with several AI labs and cloud computing operators.

Nvidia's market position has nonetheless made it an industry force and helped CEO Jensen Huang develop a relationship with Trump, who has touted American AI. Huang and Trump have made frequent appearances together, with the CEO joining the president's diplomatic trip to China. Trump, who has disclosed owning Nvidia stock, separately awarded Huang the National Medal of Science for advancing AI hardware.

Trump critics have previously accused the administration of political intervention at the DOJ, which the administration has disputed. Such intervention is traditionally out of the ordinary.

Staff-led investigations at the DOJ often take years and can stretch from one administration to the next. In addition, the DOJ routinely seeks input from companies when evaluating proposed mergers. "It would be inappropriate for the Department to conduct a merger investigation under the guise of a conduct investigation," the DOJ spokesperson said.

SCRUTINY OF OTHER NVIDIA DEALS

The DOJ has scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its 2025 deal to license technology from chip startup Groq and hire its engineers, the people said. Officials have explored whether Nvidia unfairly offered larger allocations of AI chips if customers purchased its networking equipment and Groq processors, raising questions about whether Nvidia used its dominant product to push into a newer market, the people said.

Nvidia declined to comment, and Groq did not respond to a request for comment.

The DOJ has also looked at Nvidia's acquisition of Run:ai, which makes software that helps AI chips run more efficiently, the people said.

The department's questions about the proposed Hugging Face acquisition include identifying how Nvidia might use the AI platform to harm rivals in the AI market, and whether Nvidia could use the newly acquired business to gain leverage, the people said.

Officials are also asking questions about Hugging Face's competitors, said the people.

items.title: US files lawsuit claiming Google wouldn't give employee new job following military leave

image.alt: A Google logo at a company research facility in Mountain View, California, U.S., April 15, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria

items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The US filed a lawsuit accusing Google of failing to give an employee his old job back or find him a similar job after he took one year of military leave as a US Army reservist.

Thursday's lawsuit in Manhattan federal court is a rare instance of the US government suing a private employer for violating the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994 (USERRA), which protects the civilian employment of military personnel called to active duty.

According to the complaint, Mark Davisson spent 2-1/2 years before taking military leave as a Google key account executive, handling cloud services accounts for asset manager BlackRock and hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and managing the US business of the former Credit Suisse.

Upon Davisson's return from leave in May 2023, Google allegedly refused to let him handle any customer accounts, depriving him of career advancement though he kept his pay and title.

EMPLOYEE FIRED AFTER FURTHER MILITARY LEAVE

The complaint said Google assigned Davisson in January 2024 to a cloud solutions position that also involved no management of customer accounts, and fired him seven months later as part of a broader workforce reduction and following another military leave.

Davisson, a Bronze Star and Meritorious Service Medal recipient, has a home in Charlotte, North Carolina, but lived and worked in Manhattan while Google employed him, the complaint said. Google's parent Alphabet is based in Mountain View, California.

"We disagree with the claims in this complaint," Google spokesman Atle Erlingsson said in an email. "Google takes compliance with employment laws, including USERRA, seriously and investigates allegations of workplace wrongdoing."

SUPPORT FROM TRUMP'S CIVIL RIGHTS CHIEF

The lawsuit was brought by the civil rights unit of the US Attorney's office in Manhattan, with backing from Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, the Trump administration's top civil rights enforcer.

It seeks to recoup lost wages and benefits as well as additional damages for Davisson, and require Google to ensure a nondiscriminatory workplace including by improving USERRA training.

"Federal law ensures that our brave soldiers, who sacrifice so much to keep us safe, are not punished by employers when they return to the civilian workforce after completing their military service," US Attorney Jamie McDonald in Manhattan said in a statement.

Reporting by Jonathan Stempel in New York; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama, David Holmes and Daniel Wallis

items.title: One injured in fire at South Carolina nuclear site; no contamination reported
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - A fire on Wednesday at a South Carolina complex that produced plutonium and tritium for nuclear weapons during the Cold War left one person with minor injuries, a US Department of Energy spokesperson said.

The spokesperson, citing officials at the Savannah River Site that includes the Savannah River National Laboratory where the fire was reported, said the fire was extinguished and no contamination has been reported. The spokesperson said the person injured was an employee who was taken to the hospital.

The Savannah River Site did not say what caused the fire.

The fire prompted a "site area emergency." The Federal Aviation Administration temporarily restricted flights in the area because of the fire, according to its website. The Savannah River Site said rail, river and ground travel in the area also was restricted and that employees not involved in emergency response or shutdown operations were sheltered as a precaution.

After producing material for nuclear weapons during the Cold War, the Savannah River National Laboratory now focuses on waste cleanup and nuclear materials management.

It was built near Jackson, South Carolina, in the early 1950s.

Reporting by Jasper Ward in Washington; editing by Donna Bryson

items.title: Eleven shot near Florida A&M university in Tallahassee
items.content_html:
Oct 25 (Reuters) - A shooting near a Florida university campus in Tallahassee on Saturday night left 11 people with gunshot wounds and another injured, authorities said.

The shooting took place near Florida Agricultural & Mechanical University's campus on Perry Street, the university said, while police counted six adults and six juveniles among the injured.

"At least three of the shooting victims have sustained serious injuries, while nine others are reported to be in stable condition," the Tallahassee police said in a statement.

Initial findings showed a "physical altercation" preceded the shooting, police said, without elaborating.

"It is especially heartbreaking to know that children are among those injured," said police chief Lawrence Revell.

The youngest of those shot was 11, the NY Post newspaper said, but police did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

An altercation at a homecoming party escalated into gunfire and a fight between two or three individuals led to shots being fired just before 8 p.m., the paper added.

Police said their violent crimes unit was investigating the circumstances.

"The safety and security of our students, faculty, and staff remain our highest priority," Florida A&M said on X.

Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus and Clarence Fernandez

items.title: Screwworm infests dog in Arizona, widening US cases
items.image_alt: New World screwworm and other botfly specimens are placed under a microscope as part of a demonstration at the Knipling-Bushland U.S. Livestock Insects Research Laboratory in Kerrville, Texas, U.S., July 14, 2026. REUTERS/Kaylee Greenlee/File Photo
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - New World screwworm, a parasitic fly that eats warm-blooded animals alive, has infested a dog in Arizona, widening cases to a third US state, the US Department of Agriculture said on Wednesday.

The first detection in Arizona was in Cochise County, which borders Mexico, according to the USDA.

The dog had a wound on its back that was infested with maggots, consistent with screwworm, and scientific testing verified the infestation, the Arizona Department of Agriculture said. The dog was receiving veterinary care, it added.

"We have been preparing for this possibility for a long while and are acting swiftly," State Veterinarian Dr. Ryan Wolker said in a statement.

The Arizona case marks the latest sign that screwworm, eradicated from the US decades ago, may be regaining a foothold despite federal efforts to contain it, complicating the USDA's attempts to reopen livestock trade with Mexico and ease record beef prices ahead of the midterm elections.

The USDA said it was restricting animal movement in a 20-km (12-mile) zone around the case, increasing surveillance of live animals and releasing sterile flies that combat screwworm in response to the infestation.

The agency halted livestock imports from Mexico last year to try to keep out screwworm, which advanced north through Mexico and Latin America. It detected screwworm in a calf in Texas in June and then confirmed additional cases in Texas and New Mexico.

As of Wednesday, the agency had reported 71 screwworm cases since June, and 18 were active, according to its website. Infestations have multiplied since last month, when there were only two active cases.

The import halt helped tighten US cattle supplies and push beef prices to record highs for American consumers, raising concerns about affordability ahead of the midterm elections.

The USDA began to resume livestock imports from Mexico in August and has restarted trade at three ports of entry in Arizona and New Mexico. The agency has said it next plans to resume imports from Mexico in Nogales, Arizona, on November 30, if conditions for safe trade are in place.

Last week, the USDA confirmed the first case of screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Texas.

Reporting by Tom Polansek, Christian Martinez and Daphne Psaledakis; Editing by Jasper Ward, Rod Nickel and Lincoln Feast.

items.title: US court reinstates 'Sunday Ticket' class action verdict against NFL
items.image_alt: NFL: New York Jets at New York Giants
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - A US federal appeals court on Friday reinstated a jury's verdict against the National Football League in an antitrust lawsuit claiming it overcharged subscribers to its Sunday Ticket game telecasts for more than a decade, but said the league can have a new trial on damages.

The ruling by the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a lower court judge in California who had thrown out a $4.7 billion verdict against the NFL after the trial in 2024.

The NFL in a statement said it is disappointed by the decision and is weighing its options for further court review of the decision. It defended the televised broadcast strategy as the "most fan-friendly distribution model" in sports and entertainment.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs — residential subscribers and commercial businesses — did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"Sunday Ticket" is the only broadcast option for NFL fans who want to watch their teams play out-of-market games.

The subscribers alleged "Sunday Ticket" prices were inflated to limit subscriptions and protect fees for distribution rights that broadcast networks paid to air games in local markets.

A Los Angeles federal jury awarded $4.6 billion in damages to residential subscribers and $96.9 million for commercial subscribers like bars and restaurants. But US District Judge Philip Gutierrez overturned the verdict in 2024, throwing out testimony by two key witnesses and finding that evidence did not support the damages.

The NFL had called the damages amount "nonsensical" and argued that the subscribers never proved with reliable evidence that the league's Sunday Ticket arrangements actually caused them any harm.

In its ruling on Friday, the appeals court concluded the trial judge was wrong to reject the plaintiffs' expert witnesses. A jury verdict "must stand unless it is clearly not supported by the evidence," the appeals court said.

But the panel said the jury's damages award was based "on its improper consideration of the evidence rather than according to the district court's instructions."

Reporting by Mike Scarcella; Editing by David Bario and Chizu Nomiyama

items.title: Cyberattack concealed political spending by big donors before US midterm elections
items.image_alt: "Cyber Attack Detected" phrase and PHP code appears in this illustration taken October 22, 2026. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The Federal Election Commission restored its electronic filing system Wednesday night after taking it offline for nearly 41 hours to contain a cyberattack, which temporarily concealed spending from big donors as political donations ramp up in the final days of the midterms.

Campaign watchdogs sounded alarms as the outage dragged into its third evening. Super PACs and other groups could not file mandatory 24- and 48-hour reports that show how much money they are spending to help or hurt candidates at the polls, shrouding the most recent political spending from public view.

"We didn't have access to the last-minute spending, which is really ramped up as the election draws nearer," said campaign finance watchdog Molly White, who tracks crypto and Big Tech political spending. "We have no visibility into that when the filing systems are down."

"It's pretty devastating this close to the election," she added.

The outage came at a critical time as daily spending accelerates to its fastest pace in the two-year election cycle, campaign finance experts said. Super PACs, which can accept and give unlimited amounts of money, and dark money groups spent an average of over $50 million per day the week before the outage, OpenSecrets research director Brendan Glavin said. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added.

The FEC told users that most of the services affected by the outage have been restored. It posted a notice just after 10 p.m. ET on Monday saying it was investigating a problem that caused "major" outages across its systems that process electronic campaign filings.

Reuters could not establish the motive for the hacking effort. Hackers of all stripes regularly target government networks for espionage, financial gain or political motives.

The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.

"Disclosure delayed is disclosure denied," Hilary Braseth, executive director of nonpartisan campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets, said in a statement released before the system was restored. "When hundreds of millions of dollars in outside money flood political airwaves in the final days before an election, transparency is not an optional luxury, it is a fundamental public safeguard."

The FEC did not return requests for comment Wednesday and did not announce any details on the cause of the outage. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI both referred questions to the FEC.

An FEC officer told campaign compliance firms late Monday that it took those services offline after a "bad actor" tried to breach the agency's systems, according to an email reviewed by Reuters.

Campaign finance managers had to reset their passwords before logging in to the system, according to an email reviewed by Reuters.

The timing of the hacking attempt this close to the November 3 elections, and lack of information from the FEC, stirred up conspiracy theories throughout the industry, several people said. White noted that it would be a good way for unscrupulous actors to hide unpopular last-minute spending.

"It's hard to say with any real information that that's what happened, but it's certainly I think where people's minds go very quickly," she said.

Kyle Sandy, the cybersecurity director at IT security firm Logically, said taking the system offline is the right call when dealing with an attack.

"It tells me the FEC detected something they couldn't immediately scope and chose a known outage over an unknown risk," Sandy said, giving the agency time to ensure none of its data was altered by the hackers before bringing it back online.

Reporting by Dawn Kopecki. Editing by Michael Learmonth and Stephen Coates

items.title: The midterms' final stretch: High stakes, bizarre distractions
items.image_alt: Supporters listen to US President Donald Trump speak during a Republican campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa, US, October 22, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci
items.content_html:
Oct 29 (Reuters) - After trips to Texas, Kentucky, Ohio and Iowa on the midterm campaign trail, what stayed with me were the doubts creeping in among some of Trump's most loyal supporters. In Iowa, voters at his rally told me he needed to end the Iran war and that rising gas prices were hurting him politically. Yet as Election Day approaches, much of the campaign remains consumed by debates over President Donald Trump, cultural grievances and partisan attacks, raising the question of whether either party is addressing voters' anxieties.

Five days until Election Day, and Democrats are promising to hold Trump accountable, Republicans are warning of socialism, and the president is talking about everything from crowd sizes and White House renovations to the physical appearance of allies and rivals.

Tens of millions of Americans have already voted, and even with many minds made up, both parties are making their final pitch before November 3.

Democrats want control of Congress to rein in Trump and lower living costs. Republicans warn that Democrats won't lower costs but will instead usher in socialism, destroy the country and allow what they call "transgender ideology" to spread in schools.

Trump, whose approval rating is hovering near the lowest point of his second term, has spent weeks holding near-daily rallies to help Republicans keep Congress. But his speeches often stray far from voters' economic concerns. Alongside attacks on Democrats and boasts about crowd sizes, Trump has developed a fascination with other people's bodies.

He has admired Republican Senator Jon Husted's muscular backside and enormous hands, praised Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for having the body of a 30-year-old and commented on rapper Nicki Minaj's backside. On Tuesday, he was less impressed by Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, joking that his body might not "qualify" for inspection.

At a Georgia rally Saturday, Trump brushed aside concerns about rising gas prices caused by the Iran war, arguing that higher oil prices were enriching the country. "I don't give a damn. I'm gonna say it. We're making a freaking fortune," he said.

Trump repeatedly promises gas prices will fall when the war ends, drawing applause, but says little about the living costs that voters say are their top concern.

Former President Barack Obama joined the fray over the weekend, mocking Trump's White House renovations. "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Obama told a Michigan crowd. Obama's remarks underscored how Trump continues to dominate the closing arguments of both parties. Trump told Republicans to pretend he is on the ballot next Tuesday, and Democrats have been happy to oblige.

Republicans, meanwhile, are targeting progressive candidates, immigration and cultural issues. In Michigan, attacks on Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is Muslim, have made religion and identity central to that critical race.

The focus on identity extends beyond the campaign trail. Trump's Justice Department has been aggressively attempting to stop some states from counting the ballots of people it says are noncitizens, drawing accusations from Democrats, election officials and voting-rights advocates that the federal government is seeking to insert itself into the electoral process.

Taken together, the final days of the campaign have become a debate not just about policy but about Trump himself and the reach of his presidency.

The results on Tuesday - if Democrats do as well as some polls are forecasting - could mark the beginning of Trump's lame-duck presidency and expose the limits of his political power.

TOP US POLITICS HEADLINES

  • Farmer-funded attack ads targeting Republicans air across rural America
  • Insight: Nevada unions, politicians caught between AI job creation and destruction

  • Trump expands hunt for noncitizen voters with broad subpoena campaign before midterms

  • Exclusive: US political candidates tailor messages for AI models used by voters

THE VIEW FROM BRAZIL

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Sunday, defeating Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. But Flavio refused to concede and, days later, fled to Miami after defying a court order to surrender his passports. Trump welcomed his arrival and questioned Brazil's election, calling it "very strange."

The episode has echoes of Jair Bolsonaro's departure for Florida after his 2022 defeat. And it raises fresh questions about how Lula and Trump will manage an already strained relationship.

WHAT TO WATCH FOR

November 1: Trump rally in Dubuque, Iowa
November 3: Election Day

Reporting by Nandita Bose; Editing by Ross Colvin and Alistair Bell

items.title: Walmart cuts holiday meal basket price to $3.50 per person
items.image_alt: A Walmart logo appears in this illustration taken August 18, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration
items.content_html:
Oct 28 (Reuters) - Retail giant Walmart (WMT.O) on Wednesday unveiled its holiday meal basket price at $3.50 per person, the lowest since the retailer launched the program in 2022 at a time US shoppers are facing persistent inflation and wider economic uncertainty.

  • The basket, which is meant for 10 people, includes 26 items, such as Butterball turkey, mashed potato and gravy, cranberry sauce and pumpkin pie
