items.title: Dolores Huerta, US labor leader and force for human rights, dies at 96
items.image_alt: Dolores Huerta attends the WIF (Women In Film) Honors 2025 at the Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills, California, U.S., November 6, 2025. REUTERS/Mario Anzuoni
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) with Cesar Chavez and fought legislators and powerful growers in the US to improve the lives of a previously powerless constituency, died on Wednesday at the age of 96, her family said in a statement.

Huerta was one of the foremost women in US labor history, serving the UFW as chief negotiator, strike organizer, lobbyist and reformer during its heyday in the 1960s and '70s in California's agriculture-rich Central Valley.

Thanks to the contracts the UFW negotiated, farmworkers won job security, healthcare, retirement plans, a credit union and job-specific benefits such as guaranteed rest periods, toilets in the fields, clean drinking water and protection from pesticides.

Huerta was credited with giving the UFW its slogan "Si, se puede," the loose translation of which, "Yes, we can," was later used by Barack Obama during his successful 2008 presidential campaign.

She remained a regular on the college lecture circuit into her 90s, speaking out against the immigration policies of President Donald Trump. During elections she traveled the country, endorsing candidates and registering voters.

UFW co-founder Chavez, who died in 1993 and was the face of the organization, was a seventh-grade dropout and former grape picker with a man-of-the-soil appeal who espoused the non-violent philosophies of Gandhi and Martin Luther King, with a nod to Emiliano Zapata, a leader of Mexico's peasant revolution in the early 20th century.

But Chavez had a dark side. In 2026, Huerta was one of a number of women who came forward with accounts of how they had been sexually assaulted by him, in some cases when they were minors. Huerta said that he had pressured her into having sex one time, and another time raped her. Both encounters resulted in pregnancies, and Huerta said she arranged for the babies to be raised by others.

OUT OF THE SPOTLIGHT

While Chavez was recruiting, going on well-publicized hunger strikes and being embraced by liberal lawmakers and celebrities, the diminutive, college-educated Huerta handled negotiating with growers, lobbying legislators and other business for the UFW.

She was arrested more than 20 times, subjected to death threats and other harassment. She suffered broken ribs and a damaged spleen when beaten by baton-wielding San Francisco police in a 1988 protest against the policies of George H.W. Bush during his presidential campaign.

In an interview with PBS in 2012, before the assault accusations against Chavez came to light, Huerta said she had been fine with him taking the spotlight as she wanted to focus on helping people rather than gaining fame.

"He said, 'One of us is going to have to be the spokesperson. Are you all right if I'm the spokesperson?' Of course, I said yes."

STANDING UP

Huerta was born in Dawson, New Mexico, to a Mexican immigrant family, and spent much of her youth in Stockton, California, after her parents divorced. Her father was a miner, laborer, union activist and state lawmaker; her mother raised three children while buying and running a hotel for low-income people in Stockton.

Huerta's mother instilled a spirit of activism in her daughter. Huerta was into her second marriage when she became a schoolteacher, but that career did not last long.

"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children."

She registered voters in Stockton and founded the Agricultural Workers Association before meeting Chavez and joining him in starting the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. In 1965 they began a series of strikes and boycotts that would last five years against various California grape growers and eventually spread to lettuce growers.

During that period the organization evolved into the United Farm Workers and picked up support from King and New York Senator Robert F. Kennedy. Not eating a grape — unless it had a union label — became a political statement in the United States.

The boycotts and strikes sometimes became contentious. In addition to industry opposition, the UFW found itself up against California Governor Ronald Reagan, who denounced the UFW as immoral and made a point of eating grapes on television.

COLLECTIVE BARGAINING

One by one, growers began signing contracts with the UFW and in 1975 Huerta's work also helped bring about another victory — passage of the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, the first law in the US that gave farmworkers collective bargaining rights.

Huerta said that being a woman gave her an edge at the negotiating table with growers.

"They really didn't know how to respond because they couldn't do the usual forceful type of thing," she told PBS. "And when you would bring up to them and show them the conditions that the workers were working under, and they were kind of embarrassed, actually."

In 2012, Obama presented Huerta with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian award.

Her life was the basis of the award-winning film "Dolores" that was shown at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017.

While the UFW's influence abated, Huerta's activism did not. In 2002 she established the Dolores Huerta Foundation for community activism with her daughter Camila Chavez as its executive director. She pushed for changes in immigration laws, voter registration, women's rights and Obama's healthcare reform.

Huerta, who said she remained close to the two children she had with Chavez, also had two children from her first marriage, five from her second and four from a long-term relationship with Richard Chavez, brother of Cesar and another key UFW figure, who died in 2011.

items.title: Democrats recruited spoilers in Alaska Senate race, NYT says
items.image_alt: Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan and Democratic US Senate candidate Mary Peltola participate in a debate in Anchorage, Alaska, US, October 15, 2026. REUTERS/Kerry Tasker/File Photo
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Democrats recruited potential spoilers in Alaska's US Senate race, the New York Times reported on Wednesday.

Aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee, worked with the campaign's lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats' campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan, according to the Times.

Alaska's ranked-choice ballot will feature Sullivan, Peltola, a retired teacher whose name is also Dan Sullivan and a longshot candidate named Gerald Heikes, who has run for governor and the US House of Representatives multiple times. Heikes replaced Democrat David Leslie after the progressive candidate was urged to withdraw.

Elisa Rios, Peltola's former campaign manager, told the newspaper that Peltola was aware of the effort but not directly involved. Representatives for Peltola and Elias Law Group, whose attorneys represent Peltola, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied involvement.

"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns – including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," said Monica Robinson, a spokesperson for Senate Democrats' campaign arm.

Republican super PACs during the primary sought to boost a third-party candidate who lives in Arizona. A Democratic super PAC did the same for Heikes and another Republican candidate.

The US Department of Justice preemptively filed suit in federal court last week to block certification of Alaska's election results if Sullivan narrowly loses his reelection bid. Lawyers for Peltola's campaign have asked the judge to dismiss the Trump administration's lawsuit.

Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was calling for a state investigation into whether any laws were broken, writing on X overnight: "The evidence will determine what happens next."

Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, meaning Democrats would need to pick up four seats in the November 3 midterm elections to win control of the chamber.

Alaska, a state Republican President Donald Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024, is one of several battlegrounds that will determine which party holds the Senate for the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill in Washington; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Bill Berkrot

items.title: Biden-era officials who quit over Gaza urge 2028 candidates to denounce policy architects
items.image_alt: Palestinian children walk amid the rubble of buildings destroyed during the war in Gaza City, October 7, 2026. REUTERS/Mahmoud Issa/File Photo
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - US officials who had resigned from former President Joe Biden's administration over his Gaza policy said on Wednesday that Democratic presidential candidates for the 2028 race should denounce that policy and its architects.

  • Twelve former US officials who quit the Biden administration between late 2023 and mid-2024 over US support for Israeli attacks on Gaza signed a joint statement
  • "We call on candidates for the 2028 Presidential Nomination to commit to not hire any administration official directly responsible for enabling Israel's military actions in Gaza," they said in the statement released on Wednesday.
  • A video released with the statement showed images of Biden-era officials like former Secretary of State Antony Blinken and former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, among others.
  • The Democratic Biden administration had faced protests from some progressive lawmakers and activists over the Gaza policy.
  • Progressive Democrats like US Representative Rashida Tlaib and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani have opposed US support for Israel over Israeli attacks in Gaza and Lebanon, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close ties to Republicans, leading to an erosion of Democratic backing for Washington's ally.
  • The 12 former officials said the 2028 presidential candidates should "acknowledge the complicity of the United States government in Israel's genocide in Gaza."
  • Multiple rights groups, experts, scholars and UN inquiries have assessed that Israel's devastating assault on Gaza amounts to genocide.
  • Israel has called its actions self-defense after a deadly attack by Hamas-led militants on Israel in October 2023.
  • Blinken and Sullivan have expressed concerns about civilian killings in Gaza even as the Biden administration maintained diplomatic and military support for Israel.

Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Aurora Ellis

items.title: AI-related investment, consumers likely boosted US economic growth in third quarter
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - US economic growth likely accelerated in the third quarter as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.

The anticipated strength would stand in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment. The Commerce Department will publish its advance estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product on Thursday, less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

"People are very upset about high energy and food prices, and yet the fundamentals for consumers are still decent," said Gus Faucher, chief economist at PNC Financial. "We still have job growth, wage gains and there's the strong stock market that's supporting spending by high-income households, in particular, so consumers continue to increase their spending at a pretty steady clip."

GDP likely increased at a 3.2% annualized rate last quarter, a Reuters survey of economists predicted. The economy grew at a 2.2% pace in the April-June quarter. But the survey was conducted before the release on Wednesday of September's advance economic indicators report, which showed a widening of the goods trade deficit as strong demand for capital goods linked to the AI spending boom lifted imports to a record high.

Economists estimated the trade shortfall subtracted at least 4 percentage points from GDP growth last quarter. But the drag was probably blunted by the AI-related investment, with business spending on equipment expected to have notched a third straight quarter of double-digit growth.

AI also likely contributed to spending on intellectual property products. Inventories are also expected to have added to GDP growth last quarter.

Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did not expect this to hinder the economy.

"There's likely to be more discretion when it comes to investment in AI, but the underlying momentum remains quite strong," said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon. "AI-related investment is likely to remain a key pillar of US economic activity, even if there are some risks of pullbacks and some questions as to the return on all of its investment."

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. The US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."

Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters that "economic activity is expanding at a strong pace," noting that "while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient."

ROBUST CONSUMER SPENDING EXPECTED

Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, is projected to have increased at above a 3.0% pace after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historic low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation.

Households have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, economists anticipated that consumer spending would pull back.

"It appears that households made a judgment when the conflict began earlier this year that the run-up in energy prices would prove mostly temporary," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "That assessment may prove wrong, so consumers may need, at some point, to tighten their belts."

Rising mortgage rates because of the Middle East conflict are expected to have pushed residential investment back into contraction last quarter. Higher borrowing costs have overshadowed a moderation in house prices, putting homeownership out of the reach of young adults.

Homebuilding is also being constrained by land and labor shortages amid an immigration crackdown, and higher prices for materials due to tariffs on imports. The construction of data centers to support AI likely lifted business investment in nonresidential structures after stabilizing in the second quarter. A rebound in government spending is anticipated.

A measure of domestic demand, which excludes inventories, trade and government, is expected to have surged last quarter. Final sales to private domestic purchasers grew at a 4.6% rate in the second quarter.

"The overall picture is that the economy is growing at a decent pace, but the primary factors are an AI-driven investment boom and consumption driven primarily by rising stock wealth," said Dean Baker, senior economist at the Center for Economic and Policy Research. "It's unclear how long this can continue, but this is not a very stable picture, nor a very positive one for most working people."

Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Andrea Ricci

items.title: Canada reports limited progress in trade talks with US
items.image_alt: Canadian and U.S. flags fly on both sides of the St. Clair River near the Blue Water Bridge, connecting Sarnia, Ontario, and Port Huron, Michigan, in Sarnia, Ontario, Canada, September 2, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Osorio
items.content_html:
Summary:

  • Trump widened trade rift with Canada with steep tariffs
  • Canada's Carney sees a "slight intensification" in talks
  • Carney says Canada wants deal that works for both nations

OTTAWA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - There has been limited progress in trade talks with the United States to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, a Canadian government official with knowledge of the discussions said on Wednesday.

US President Donald Trump widened a trade rift by imposing 50% tariffs on a wide range of imports from Canada in August, accusing the US neighbor to the north of discriminatory treatment of American goods. Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs.

Reuters reported on Monday that the two countries were working on a trade deal. Talks on a broader agreement stalled in August when Canada walked away from the negotiating table.

"While discussions have continued, there has been limited progress," the Canadian official told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who on Monday said there had been "a slight intensification" in talks, reiterated on Wednesday that Canada is ready to sign an agreement that is in the interests of both nations.

"If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them, but we're not at that position right now," Carney told reporters.

A US government official said on Wednesday there were significant ongoing talks, including between US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for trade with the United States.

The White House said the Office of the US Trade Representative and the Commerce Department are continuing to work together on key issues involving trade with Canada, and that both Lutnick and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have had discussions with their Canadian counterparts in recent days.

Trump's Republican Party is fighting to retain control of the US Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a for the US president, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada.

Some experts have said the Trump administration may be less willing to make trade concessions to Canada after the midterms.

The latest talks have focused on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including up to a 50% tariff on Canadian steel and a 25% tariff on autos. The Commerce Department, which administers the Section 232 tariffs, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump on Sunday said the trade dispute would be resolved "soon," without providing specifics.

Trump signed an order last week to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from Maine, where incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins is locked in a tight reelection race. Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50% tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order.

Reporting by Promit Mukherjee, David Shepardson and David Ljunggren; Writing by Caroline Stauffer. Editing by Tomasz Janowski and Will Dunham.

items.title: US closes $5.1 billion loan to Alliant Energy for new gas power generation, energy storage
items.image_alt: Alliant Energy's coal plant in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, U.S. on the shore of Lake Michigan, July 4, 2022. REUTERS/Timothy Gardner
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The US Department of Energy said on Wednesday it has closed a $5.1 billion loan package to Alliant Energy (LNT.O) to expand power generation and bolster the grid at plants in Iowa and Wisconsin.

The 30-year loans will support new natural gas-fired power plants, systems to store energy using batteries, and upgrades to existing generation facilities, it said. They will also create hundreds of construction-related jobs and deliver more than 2.6 gigawatts of new or upgraded power generation capacity, it said. That's enough power for nearly 1.8 million homes.

Lisa Barton, president and CEO of Alliant, said in a statement that the financing helps lower the cost of building power generation capacity and infrastructure while strengthening the grid and supporting long-term savings. Alliant, based in Wisconsin, said it projects that over the lifetime of the loans, customers would save up to $1.2 billion in power bills.

The loan had originally been proposed by the administration of former President Joe Biden, in his last days in office in January 2025, when it was only a conditional loan of $3 billion.

The office of Energy Dominance Financing, called the Loan Programs Office under Biden, has hundreds of billions of dollars in financing available, the bulk of which Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said will support nuclear power.

More than the name of the office has changed. Its mission during the Biden administration was to provide support to emerging clean energy projects and alternative vehicles that struggled to get bank loans. Now it includes support to projects such as natural gas that have typically been able to get bank loans. Energy storage, which typically includes batteries, was supported in both the initial and the closed loan.

"By bringing new, dependable power online, we are strengthening our nation's energy security and lowering electricity costs for families and businesses across Iowa and Wisconsin," the loan office director, Gregory Beard, said in a release.

Any lowering of electricity costs could take many years as the loans take place over decades.

items.title: US Supreme Court denies immigration judges the power to shelve deportation cases
items.image_alt: A view of the US Supreme Court in Washington, DC, US, September 25, 2026. REUTERS/Nathan Howard/File Photo
items.content_html:
Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump's administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as "administrative closure," while litigation continues in the dispute.

The Supreme Court's decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision.

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day.

Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule's invalidation. In a statement, the litigants and the lawyers representing them from the liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment in Tuesday's decision.

"Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country," they said in the statement.

"This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny," they added.

Representatives from the Justice Department and the Texas attorney general's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty.

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF CASES

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump's hardline approach toward immigrants.

In 2024, Biden's administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump's first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges "effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country."

Trump's administration and the state then jointly asked US District Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O'Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O'Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O'Connor's decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump's administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using "manufactured litigation" with "ideologically aligned" Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

"The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception," they wrote.

Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; editing by Will Dunham
